Use only the tools exposed for this stage. Use read_documents to batch several needed pages in one call, avoiding repeated model round-trips. Use the supplied stage-scoped catalog; do not read arbitrary paths or earlier runs. The originating study and its explanations remain hidden. For case units, definitions or processing facts, use request_case_definition; an isolated service releases only reviewed neutral facts with opaque evidence IDs. General literature retrieval remains restricted to independently dated earlier sources. You may reason conditionally while a case fact remains unknown. Use search_sources for actual missing public knowledge; returned access depth is explicit, not proof of relevance. analyze_csv reads every selected row, not the 12-row preview. Submit once using submit_result; if validation fails, the draft is saved locally. Use patch_result with the latest draft_ref and only changed fields; do not regenerate unchanged text. Original submissions remain archived. Every result requires summary (nonempty string) and artifacts, evidence, claims, limitations, next_actions (arrays, empty allowed), plus stage-specific fields. For development_step focus/uptake source, use a supplied source ID, document ID or unambiguous registered filename. Use a source-field locator instead of copying an exact quote when convenient. A registered document ID/path suffices if no specific field is selected; optional paraphrases are stored separately from exact quotes. For a JSON source, quote the exact string VALUE, without adding its field name. Alternatively supply quote_pointer (JSON pointer to a string) and omit quote; the exact selected string will be resolved and logged. For learning_request, context_ref="development_step" may replace duplicate gap/why_now strings; this references your own gap/reason, never changes its content. For sources[].local_path use the returned D-document ID to avoid copying long paths; it resolves to the exact registered file. source_use covers exactly broker_reply_source_ids, not the whole source catalog or new searches in this turn. Cite newly read tool sources in evidence/memory_notes with actual paths/URLs. Keep result text concise; use 0-1 useful memory notes unless multiple are necessary. Preserve branches and open issues. files is an object of relative artifact paths to complete text content; every declared artifact must exist or be provided in files. If artifacts is empty, your exact summary is saved automatically as an artifact; do not repeat the entire JSON as prose. For review-index-v2, start with the stage directory and read relevant result/before-input sections by document ID. Summaries are incomplete navigation excerpts, not evidence. Start with input_refs and inline bodies, not the entire provenance catalog. When reading a needed document, request the relevant JSON pointer or a useful page (up to 12000 characters); avoid repeated tiny probes. For review, source_stage must match the stage containing the exact quote; note_keys are actual memory_notes keys (often empty), not JSON field names. If an input body is omitted or represented by $document, read it by ID. No scientific text was summarized; originals and before-inputs remain readable. Online retrieval is enabled.

Execute agent_learn.md's learning and co-questioning plan. Chinese readable artifacts.
Do not read earlier project runs/candidates. Only use listed inputs, their cited source files,
the current case's exchanges, supplied memory, and public sources. A previous task is accessible
only through the supplied memory packet and its provenance. Do not scan old run directories.
Read the actual common sources behind summaries. Treat published findings as published knowledge.
Do not present them as discoveries. Preserve disagreements and all idea branches.
Use public sources via urllib/curl (Crossref, Europe PMC, PMC, arXiv, publishers as accessible).
Save retrieved text and exact URLs; distinguish full text, abstract and failed access.
No solving, scientific validation experiment, proof or novelty gate is required for ideas.
Small worked calculations are allowed to learn a concept, clearly labelled learning examples.
Save result.json with the six runtime fields plus the requested fields. Use summary as a STRING.
Do not spend your entire budget retrieving; save useful partial understanding if needed.

Continue as domain_scientist. Read the available actual independent initial notes and any earlier peer reply.
Address the peer's specific question. Explain a concept mismatch, a useful connection or a
disagreement. You may redefine the shared object and change the question. Do not just review.
Save EXCHANGE.md. Return shared_object, response_to_peer, disagreement (strings), and learning_request:
{needed: boolean, gap: string, why_now: string, search_terms: [strings]}.
The request must arise from this exchange; if no meaningful gap exists, set needed=false.


Also return memory_notes: 0-3 reusable notes; [] when unchanged. Each object has:
key (stable lower_case ASCII concept key; reuse an existing key when correcting it), title,
kind (source_knowledge/interpretation/hypothesis/correction),
mastery (read/explained/used; identify how the knowledge informed actual research when used),
understanding, conditions, open_questions (nonempty strings), optional example (text or null),
tags (array, include English and Chinese terms), sources (array of actual URLs or source paths),
revision_reason (required when the key already exists).
Separate published knowledge, your inference and untested hypotheses. 'Unknown' is a valid
open_questions string, never invent competence. Describe corrections explicitly.
Also return memory_use: array of {key,source_task,used_for,scope_check} for notes actually used;
return [] if none. State what you still cannot explain/use.


HYPOTHESIS DEVELOPMENT v3:
Use your disciplinary understanding and screened long-term memory to develop assumptions.
Start from a specific phenomenon, tension, difficulty or missing relation. When you have a
possible explanation or organizing principle, state what you suppose; merely changing a
'whether' question into an affirmative sentence adds no insight. An assumption can be an
explanation, conjectured relation, representation, distinction or method/construction principle.
Explore what conceptual move it makes and, CONDITIONALLY on the assumption, what changes in
our understanding or possible actions. Develop concrete consequences, not promises of impact.
Use these as thinking moves, not a checklist that every early idea must already satisfy.
Before requesting learning, identify a specific missing conceptual connection in the current
assumption, why it matters, and what understanding might change. Return to that same gap after
reading: explain a revised premise, relation or conditional consequence, or retain the gap.
Do not substitute more citations, caveats, controls or formal wording for conceptual development.
Measurement/method contributions remain valid when their concrete intellectual consequences are
articulated. No compulsory mechanism, scientific breakthrough, or progress at each turn.

In peer discussion, engage a specific assumption: elaborate a consequence, expose a hidden
premise, connect a disciplinary concept, propose a distinct explanation, or revise a relation.
Explain the reasoning. You may retain, revise, branch, or park your own line. No forced consensus,
disagreement, novelty claim, completed hypothesis or compulsory new branch each turn.
Evidence strength, proof, available data/tools, implementation and experimental feasibility
are NOT requirements for proposing, retaining or prioritizing a hypothesis. Do not turn
discussion into a feasibility review. Research/analysis requests remain optional resources
for thinking. Correct concrete errors in premises while keeping conditional hypotheses distinct
from established observations; lack of evidence alone is not a refutation.

hypothesis_state.self contains your saved branches; peer_branches belong to their named owners.
Return hypothesis_updates: [] when nothing changed, otherwise full cards:
{key: stable local identifier [A-Za-z0-9_]+, base_version: 0 for new or supplied own version,
assumption: nonempty provisional claim, motivation: specific phenomenon/difficulty/relation,
conceptual_move: string or null if still unclear,
implications: [specific conditional consequences, may be empty],
open_questions: [unresolved conceptual questions, may be empty],
status: developing/parked, reason: why propose/change/park/resume,
influenced_by: [exact ref objects from supplied hypothesis_state],
depends_on: [exact supplied hypothesis refs used as premises; [] if none]}.
Influence is not logical dependence. Declare depends_on only for actual premises; do not invent
links. revision_obligations lists your branches whose declared premises changed or themselves
await review. This does NOT mean the branch is false. For each obligation return
 dependency_responses:[{ref:exact hypothesis_ref,action:revise/reaffirm/park/unresolved,reason}].
Reaffirm/revise requires an updated full card citing current dependency versions; changing only
links is recorded as provenance maintenance, not conceptual progress. Park/unresolved retains
the branch and its warning. Reasoned reaffirmation is valid; do not mechanically follow criticism.
Dependencies not explicitly declared cannot be inferred by this structural checker.
Omitting a branch retains it. To keep an alternative, use a new key and cite the parent ref;
never overwrite a peer's branch. Missing conceptual_move or implications is allowed for an
early assumption. Keep hypothetical consequences explicitly hypothetical, including examples.
Reusable conceptual learning can also be saved through existing memory_notes, kind:hypothesis,
with actual source provenance and same-key revisions. Run-local branches do not replace your
long-term disciplinary memory or its source screening. Do not invent empirical support.


Optional learning_request: {needed:boolean, gap, why_now, queries:[strings],
urls:[], source_ids:[], record_ids:[], operations:[], case_questions:[]}.
Use case_questions for actual case definitions/units/processing order; literature cannot
reconstruct undocumented case facts. These questions dispatch even when needed:false.
General theory and explanation-development requests use queries/gap. For case facts, the
isolated material service releases supported neutral definitions, not hidden conclusions.
The controller searches and returns actual readable content. Keep your own scientific query;
classify returned sources as directly relevant, transferable method, or irrelevant, with reasons.
Do not treat a successful download as understanding. No compulsory tool use.
For a small worked calculation use an operation {kind:"calculation", question,
bindings:{name: numeric scalar/array}, expression: numeric array expression,
expected: optional numeric value/array}. Available arithmetic, slices and named functions
include mean,sum,std,norm,diff,abs,sqrt. Define which rows/columns mean which entities.
Top-level analysis_plan also dispatches. needed:false disables literature search, not explicit
calculations. Unsupported requests return a pending capability task; no scientific rejection.
Keep purely tentative proposals in hypothesis_updates/next_actions, not execution fields.


HYPOTHESIS CONTENT CYCLE:
Use development_cycle as a thinking context, not a demand to invent progress. Choose one
specific explanatory relation, construction, distinction or unresolved phenomenon from its
sources. Locate the conceptual gap: what connection/premise/consequence is still unclear?
Choose a next move because of this gap: learn, derive, connect, reframe, or hold. Explain why
that move could change understanding. For learning, use this gap in learning_request.gap and
why_now, and formulate targeted queries; do not request a broad survey merely to fill a stage.
In discussion, take up a peer's concrete relation and explain how your discipline extends,
challenges or changes its consequences. Generic agreement about controls or feasibility is
not a substitute; a measurement contribution is valid when its specific consequences matter.
Study returned services against the gap that requested them, including failures and pending
capabilities. Do not call retrieval success learning. If nothing changes, say so and preserve
the gap. Own previous_steps carry unfinished thinking across phases and sessions. When the
controller flags repeated_no_change, reconsider the missing connection, premise, or next
learning move; holding a branch is valid. The flag uses supplied peer content comparisons, not a quality verdict. A shared interpretation is normal.
Return development_step:{focus:{source:exact development_cycle.sources key,quote:exact excerpt},
gap:nonempty text, action:learn/derive/connect/reframe/hold, reason:nonempty text,
expected_change:text or null for hold,
uptake:[{source:exact source key,quote:exact excerpt or null only for unresolved,
effect:revise/extend/challenge/unchanged/unresolved,reason:how this affects the focus,
consequence:conditional consequence or null when none follows}],
outcome:{kind:relation/implication/clarification/unchanged/uncertain,
statement:what changed or did not, remaining_gap:text or null}}.
Account once for EACH service key in required_service_uptake. If peer_sources is nonempty,
engage at least one (unresolved with a reason is valid). Other uptake is optional. Quotes must
come from the named source; for published claims quote readable source content, not metadata.
For relation/implication outcomes, preserve the resulting claim in a hypothesis_update's
assumption or implications. This records an author's proposal, NOT confirmed novelty/progress.
No compulsory new relation, branch, agreement, data, experiment, proof or implementation.


QUESTION STATE PROTOCOL v2:
question_state.self is YOUR authoritative current personal question. peer_questions belong
to their named owners. shared_question is the discussion's current shared question, or null.
Do not reconstruct your prior question from the latest peer message. The controller records
the actual before-state; do NOT return question_before or question_after.
Return personal_question_update: {base: the exact self.ref object, action: retain/revise,
question: your current or revised personal question, reason: a nonempty explanation,
influenced_by: array of exact question ref objects from this supplied packet}.
Retain means the question text stays exactly the same. Revise may include adopting a peer's
line or the shared question: explain why; use influenced_by to identify relevant question refs.
You need not preserve disagreement or a distinct personal question if you decide to change it.
Separately return shared_question_update: null, or {base: the exact shared_question.ref (null
if none yet), action: propose/revise/retain, question: shared question text, reason: nonempty,
influenced_by: array of refs from this packet}. Propose is only for a first shared question.
A shared question is a versioned proposal, not proof of peer agreement. Revising it NEVER
changes another researcher's personal question. Your own personal update is independent too.

Use controller-owned question_state, never invent question_before/question_after.
Keep hypotheses tied to specific entities/relations in this situation. A measurement or representation contribution is legitimate; explain its concrete consequences without forcing a natural mechanism.

Now I have the peer's full picture. Key content:

Peer (theory_scientist) current branches:
1. threshold_coordinate_factorization v2
2. latch_as_threshold_inequality v2
3. barrier_interaction_frontier v2
4. clamp_admissibility_limits v1
5. threshold_gap_addressability v1

Peer question (personal v2): what quantity decides (i) same-γ double flip and (ii) whether the whole cycle keeps nested RPM (graph global property or assemblable from pairwise gap conditions)?

My role as domain_scientist: peer's specific question, plus I should explain a concept mismatch, useful connection, or disagreement. I have a disciplinary angle: rigid-body statics / over-center geometry / mechanical contact. My prior line: over-center geometry γ_th = y·tanθ_stop − x_offset; and the key physical point: the two "states" are contact against hard stops, not two wells of a potential. That's a concept mismatch worth pressing: the peer talks of "势垒/半宽" as if there were a potential-well bistability; in this apparatus bistability comes from a kinematic constraint (stop contact), so "half-width h" is not an energy barrier at all; it's set by the difference of stop angles, and there's a mechanical consequence: torque balance has a *sign* condition — the rotor is pressed against the stop with a normal force that can vanish. That gives a third quantity neither b nor h: the *contact normal force* (preload) at the holding stop. This is exactly what determines whether a clamped configuration is admissible in the free device (peer's branch clamp_admissibility_limits), and also whether a "latch" is a genuine avalanche or a "slip off the stop" event.

Key idea for this turn (hypothesis development, domain_scientist): Introduce the "contact/admissibility" dimension as a genuinely third coordinate: the rotor state is not defined solely by sign(θ) but by the pair (stop contacted, sign of normal force). A rotor at +1 is in equilibrium only if the net torque pushes it into the + stop (N > 0). Once coupling makes N → 0 and change sign, the rotor leaves the stop and takes a continuous angle — a third state invisible in the ±1 encoding. The condition N_i = 0 is generally *not* the same as the switching threshold condition; it is a distinct curve in (γ, σ_j) space. And here's the useful connection/consequence: for a rotor held at its + stop with drive γ increasing, the switch condition γ = F^+ and the contact-loss condition are related: The switching threshold is exactly where N = 0 if the rotor is quasi-static and stays on the stop until the torque changes sign? Actually let me think mechanically.

Mechanics: rotor is a rigid bar on a pivot, constrained by stops at ±θ_s. The "state" +1 = pressed against + stop. Torques: drive spring, coupling spring, and stop reaction (unilateral). Equilibrium at + stop requires total torque (excluding stop) to be in the direction pushing into + stop: T_drive+coupling < 0 or > 0 with sign convention. As γ increases, the net torque at the + stop changes sign; at that zero the reaction vanishes and the rotor leaves the stop. Whether it then snaps to the − stop or finds an interior equilibrium depends on the torque for θ in between. In my over-center read, the drive spring torque vanishes at γ = γ_over-center for all θ (when the spring line passes through pivot): the torque function T(θ) = k(...)·L·R·sin(θ−φ)/ℓ... For a spring attached at distance L on the bar, the torque about the pivot is proportional to sin(θ−φ), so it *changes sign* at θ=φ where the bar is collinear with the spring line. So in the interior there can be an equilibrium at θ = φ (unstable/stable?) — that's the over-center point. So: at the + stop, the drive torque is proportional to sin(θ_s − φ). Increasing γ rotates φ. When φ passes θ_s, drive torque changes sign at the stop and pushes the rotor off. So the threshold is φ = θ_s i.e. tan φ = γ/y ... = tanθ_s ⇒ γ = y tanθ_s − x. Good, consistent with my over-center formula.

Crucially, off the stop the rotor goes to... the other stop if the torque is monotone and there's no interior stable point. The interior torque zero at θ=φ is *unstable*? Consider the torque T ∝ sin(θ−φ) which for θ slightly greater than φ is positive, pushing θ further up (away) — depends on sign convention; magnitude also ∝ R·... Actually torque = k(ℓ_d−ℓ_0)·(L R sin(θ−φ)/ℓ_d) — the factor (ℓ_d − ℓ_0) matters: if the spring is in tension (ℓ>ℓ_0), the torque is restoring toward θ=φ; if compression (ℓ < ℓ_0), it's repulsive from θ=φ. This is important! My earlier uncertainty noted "coupling spring rest lengths (2.4/2.6) and drive spring rest lengths (3.9/4.2) may give zero-crossing of spring force and torque sign reversal." That's a real mechanical subtlety: a linear spring with non-negligible rest length ℓ_0 gives torque ∝ (1 − ℓ_0/ℓ)·(LR sin(θ−φ)/ℓ) — sign depends on whether spring is in tension or compression. When ℓ crosses ℓ_0, the effective stiffness vanishes (zero-stiffness point).

So the domain contribution: the "threshold" is not where an energy barrier is overcome; it's where the *unilateral contact reaction vanishes*. Hence:
- Half-width h is not a barrier; it's the half-angle between stops mapped through the geometry. So "lowering the barrier to make switching cheap" is a category error in this device: there is no barrier at all on the stop (the state is a constraint). Easy switching = small (θ_s − φ gap) i.e., threshold near the current drive; that's gap, not height.
- Contact reaction N is the third coordinate. Two states with the same ±1 label can differ in N (preload), and N is what determines (a) whether the clamped configuration is admissible (peer branch 4) and (b) whether a stop-release is silent in the event record.

Now: how does this bear on the peer's question of "what decides (i) same-γ double flip and (ii) RPM"? A useful connection: the same-γ double flip requires the second rotor's threshold to be *crossed by the first rotor's switching event* through the b shift. But in the contact picture, there's a sharper possibility: the coupling spring transmits force through the *bar*, and when rotor j leaves its stop and rotates, the coupling spring force changes discontinuously-ish (from a stop-supported value to a path value). Actually the key mechanical fact: as long as j is held at its stop, the coupling spring force is determined by the fixed geometry; when j releases, the coupling force changes as j's angle changes. So the "b shift" measured by clamping is the *initial* value of a state-dependent coupling; the actual trigger is whether, after j's release, the torque on i at its stop changes sign *at that same drive value*. That's a finite-jump condition, not an infinitesimal one — but the sign condition is exactly the gap inequality the peer wrote. Good: the peer's inequality is right in form, and I can give it a mechanical interpretation: "same-γ double flip = the coupling-mediated jump in torque at rotor i exceeds the residual distance to i's release threshold; because both are torques from the same spring, the inequality can be written as a comparison of angular gaps rather than drive gaps." And importantly: torque equality criterion assumes quasi-static, so the double flip is not an avalanche with dynamics — it's a *co-release*: both rotors leave their stops at the same drive value, i.e., the constrained equilibrium path loses stability at a fold. That's a genuinely different concept from "avalanche/triggering" — it's a bifurcation of the constrained equilibrium set. Consequence: you can distinguish by *how many events occur per cycle* and by *whether the drive value is repeated*; but you cannot distinguish "simultaneous" from "triggered within resolution" — which the peer already noted.

Second, for RPM: peer asks whether RPM is assembled from pairwise gap conditions. My domain answer: no, and there is a specific mechanical reason: the constraint set (which stops are occupied) is a *complementarity* problem, and as the drive traverses, the sequence of contact sets is determined by the geometry of the admissible region in (γ, θ1..θ4) space. RPM asks whether the sequence of stop-contact sets under a cyclic protocol is nested. This is a property of the *arrangement of hyperplanes* (release surfaces γ = F_i^±(σ)) in the drive axis — i.e., of the ordering structure of a set of switch thresholds as a function of state. There's a known structure: a system of independent hysteron thresholds gives nested intervals; the "no-passing" condition is precisely: along any driving path, the set of thresholds not yet passed is ordered consistently — mathematically, the collection of transition surfaces forms a "no-passing" arrangement. If I introduce this as "the ordering structure of the release set," then a concrete local quantity that decides RPM in this device: whether the release thresholds are *monotone under the natural partial order of states* (i.e., F_i^+ is non-increasing in each neighbor's state or consistently signed according to coupling sign). Hmm — but per peer's literature, three interacting hysterons with pure state-dependent shifts already violate RPM in most graphs. Why? Because shifts can be "inconsistent": e.g., a rotor's up threshold can be lowered by one neighbor's +1 and raised by another's, causing non-monotone loops.

A potentially sharp conceptual contribution: in *this* device, all coupling is mediated by *linear springs*, hence the interaction is derivable from a single potential U(θ1..θ4) (a gradient/reciprocal interaction with symmetric Hessian). The b_ij in threshold coordinates is not symmetric (2.2 vs 0.6), but the underlying mechanical coupling is reciprocal. This matters for RPM: for a gradient (potential) system with unilateral constraints and a single scalar drive γ entering linearly (as −γ·F generalized force), the constrained equilibrium path is the graph of a *gradient flow* / minimization of Φ(θ;γ) = U(θ) − γ·(something). If Φ = U(θ) − γ·W(θ) with W a fixed "drive potential," then... hmm. In this device the drive force on rotor i is not independent of θ — but is it a potential? The drive spring couples the rotor to the rod: force is −∂U_spring/∂θ_i for fixed γ. So the total energy Φ(θ;γ) = Σ U_springs(θ,γ) + U_coupling(θ) is a well-defined potential for each γ, and the observed sequence of stops is the sequence of local minima of Φ as γ is swept. Then RPM becomes: does the sequence of local minima of a one-parameter family of potentials Φ(·;γ) satisfy nesting? This is a real, checkable structural claim: for a one-parameter family where γ enters *linearly* (Φ = Φ_0 − γ X), the local minima are nested in a strong sense — this is the classic "Maxwell/override" structure, and RPM-ish nesting follows for a "simple" energy landscape. Whether it holds depends on the "landscape" being free of certain fold interactions. Hmm, is this a known result? There is literature on "return point memory" in systems with a single control parameter and gradient dynamics — e.g., "hysteresis in disordered systems: return-point memory" — the classic result (Sethna et al., PRL 1993) is that RPM holds exactly when the system has a "no-passing" property, which follows for a broad class of systems with a single driving variable (the "ABBM"/interface models) but not for all interacting systems. And there's the known statement: RPM is guaranteed in systems where the dynamics is a "no-passing" cellular automaton. The domain angle: with a single common drive γ and reciprocal spring coupling (a potential), the model is in the class "one-dimensional control parameter, gradient dynamics" — for which RPM is *generic* under some conditions? Actually the literature: Preisach systems have RPM by construction. But interacting hysteron systems can break RPM. So potential/gradient structure is not sufficient. Hmm. Think of the simplest: two coupled hysterons with energy Φ = ... plus γ-linear coupling; transitions as γ increases. For a potential system with γ entering linearly, the sequence of *global* minima as γ increases is a sequence of first-order transitions; and the graph of global minima vs γ is monotone (that's a 1D Maxwell construction — the global minimum switches monotonically) — so "state vs γ" would have no hysteresis at all in the global-min case; hysteresis comes from *metastability* (local minima) — and the local-min branch structure can break RPM. So the potential structure doesn't save RPM; RPM needs no-passing among the metastable branches, which can fail when a fold of one branch is "passed" differently in different histories due to multi-element rearrangement. So I should be careful not to overclaim.

But there is a sharper, device-specific claim I can make: the *measured* quantities originate in a single energy function, so b_ij and b_ji are not independent: their asymmetry must be attributable to the *curvatures* (K_ii) at the respective stops (peer already said that: b_ij = ∂²U/∂θi∂θj / K_ii). This gives a concrete, checkable consequence: with the over-center geometry I can estimate the curvature K_ii analytically (the second derivative of the spring torque at the stop), and hence predict b_ij from the apparatus geometry alone (spring stiffnesses, L, w, stop angles). That would convert the three-coordinate decomposition from a fit into a parameter-free prediction. That's a real "measurement/derivation" contribution with concrete consequences: if the predicted b asymmetry (ratio 3.7) matches the ratio of curvatures computed from stop angles and geometry, then the "nonreciprocity" is fully explained by geometry, and the peer's branch could be *strengthened* by an independent prediction rather than a fit. Let me check whether I can compute curvatures plausibly with the given apparatus numbers, as a *learning example*.

Let me set up the drive torque quantitatively.

Rotor: bar of length? w = 15.2 cm pivot spacing. Spring attaches at distance L from pivot along the bar, and to a horizontal rod at height y = 9.4 cm above? Let's define: pivot at origin; θ measured from vertical? "Theta=0 points along y." Let me model: attachment point on bar at distance L, direction θ from y-axis? Then attachment point coordinates: (L sinθ, L cosθ) if θ from y toward x. The rod is horizontal at height y? A point on the rod at (γ, y)? Then spring vector = (γ − L sinθ, y − L cosθ), length R = sqrt((γ−L sinθ)² + (y−L cosθ)²). The torque about pivot: τ = −k(R−ℓ0)·(∂R/∂θ)... ∂R/∂θ = [ (γ−Lsinθ)(−Lcosθ) + (y−Lcosθ)(L sinθ) ] / R = L[ −γcosθ + L sinθcosθ + y sinθ − L sinθcosθ ] / R = L( y sinθ − γ cosθ )/R = L R' sin(θ − φ)/... with tanφ = γ/y. Indeed y sinθ − γcosθ = R cos? Let's define φ with tanφ=γ/y, then y sinθ − γ cosθ = √(y²+γ²) sin(θ−φ). So ∂R/∂θ = L sin(θ−φ)/R where I dropped the factor √(y²+γ²)? Let me redo: y sinθ − γ cosθ = √(y²+γ²)(cosφ sinθ − sinφ cosθ) = √(y²+γ²) sin(θ−φ). Hmm but also R² = (γ−Lsinθ)² + (y−Lcosθ)² = γ²+y²+L² −2L(γ sinθ + y cosθ). Let me redo carefully with attachment at (L sinθ, L cosθ) and rod point (γ, y):

R² = (γ − L sinθ)² + (y − L cosθ)² = γ² + y² + L² − 2L(γ sinθ + y cosθ).
∂(R²)/∂θ = −2L(γ cosθ − y sinθ) = 2L(y sinθ − γ cosθ).
So 2R ∂R/∂θ = 2L(y sinθ − γ cosθ) ⇒ ∂R/∂θ = L(y sinθ − γ cosθ)/R.
Torque about pivot from spring force on bar = −k(R−ℓ0) ∂R/∂θ = −k(R−ℓ0) L (y sinθ − γcosθ)/R.

At the stop, θ = θ_s. Threshold where torque (excluding stop reaction) = 0: either R = ℓ0 (spring at natural length, force zero — the "slack" case!) or y sinθ_s = γ cosθ_s ⇒ γ = y tanθ_s. Interesting — the threshold condition γ = y tanθ_stop is exactly the over-center condition (spring line through pivot), *independent of L, k, ℓ0*. Great, that matches my earlier formula with the x-offset (attachment offset x means the rod point is (γ + x?, y) — anyway).

So the release condition at the stop is the collinearity condition. This is the crucial mechanical point: **the release threshold is a geometric collinearity, not an energy comparison.** And the stability of the stop-pressed state is determined by the sign of the torque, which is ∝ (R−ℓ0)(y sinθ − γ cosθ)... with sign conventions. Two factors! So the "torque at stop" has two zeros: R = ℓ0 (spring unstretched — the spring passes through its natural length along the path) and the collinearity. This is the genuine mechanical nuance I flagged as an uncertainty earlier. Consequence: near R ≈ ℓ0, the effective torque vanishes and the threshold sensitivity diverges — i.e., the geometry→threshold map has a *singular* region. This bears directly on the peer's "same knob closes the gap and raises |b|": the reason |b| grows with L and the gap shrinks with L could be one and the same geometric fact, but there is a *different* mechanism available: the natural-length crossing, controlled by ℓ0 and y — an independent knob (rest length), which the peer listed as an open question ("can gap closure and |b| growth be decoupled, e.g. by changing spring stiffness or end distance?"). My answer: stiffness k does NOT change the threshold at all (it cancels in the torque-zero condition) — it only changes the *curvature* (hence b in threshold units) and dynamic speed. So changing k decouples b from the threshold gap! That's a concrete, non-obvious consequence: k is a pure "b knob" while geometry (θ_s, y, L) sets the thresholds. Let me verify: b_ij (threshold shift) = [∂²U/∂θi∂θj]/K_ii where K_ii is the torque curvature. Coupling stiffness k_c enters numerator linearly; K_ii is sum of drive-spring curvature and coupling curvature. So b ~ k_c/(k_d + k_c) roughly — indeed stiffness ratio controls b while thresholds (zeros of torque) are k-independent. So yes: b can be tuned by stiffness ratio while keeping thresholds fixed. That directly answers the peer's open question about whether the gap/coupling tension is a hard constraint: it isn't, because k_d/k_c is an independent knob that changes b but not the thresholds.

Wait, careful: K_ii includes the coupling contribution too, so changing k_c changes both numerator and denominator nonlinearly; but changing the *drive* stiffness k_d changes only the denominator ⇒ b decreases as k_d increases, at fixed thresholds. That's a clean decoupling.

This is a strong, concrete conceptual contribution: the two "functions" the peer bundled into L — b (coupling field) and threshold gap — are actually controlled by *different* mechanical parameters: the thresholds are geometric (L-independent in the collinearity sense? hmm, L doesn't even appear in γ = y tanθ_s!). Wait: that says the *intrinsic* threshold γ_th = y tanθ_s − x_offset is independent of L entirely. But data show pair_A rotor1 up threshold moves 7.3 → 5.5 as L goes 0 → 4.731, and the neighbor-state shift. So the L-dependence of the *clamped* thresholds can't come from the drive geometry alone — it must come from the coupling spring's torque at the stop, which is k_c(R_c − ℓ_c)∂R_c/∂θ and does depend on ell. And it enters as an additive torque, moving the zero. So the "clamped threshold" F^±(σ_j) = solution of T_drive(θ_s) + T_coupling(θ_s, σ_j) = 0, i.e., not simply additive in γ! Because T_drive is nonlinear in γ. Peer's additive form F = c + bσ + ±h is a linearization. Hmm — but data fit it to 0.1 cm. Fine.

But here's a consequence: in the clamped measurement (neighbor fixed at its stop), the coupling torque at rotor i's stop is *constant* (depends on fixed geometry), and shifting γ shifts the drive torque. So the shift b_i = −T_coupling(θ_i^s)/ (∂T_drive/∂γ) — a ratio of the coupling torque at the stop to the drive torque's γ-sensitivity. Crucially: **b is the coupling torque at the release configuration divided by the drive sensitivity**, so b encodes the *direction* of the coupling force at the stop, and its sign is tied to whether the coupling spring is in tension or compression at that stop. Statics: if the coupling spring at the stop is compressed (R<ℓ0) the sign flips relative to tension. Since pair_A and pair_B differ in rest length (2.4/2.6 vs 4.1) and geometry, the sign change from −0.6 to +5.6 could be a *natural-length* effect as much as a "parallel vs crossed" topology effect. That's a real alternative explanation of the sign flip the peer attributes to geometry (af) — and it's testable from the numbers: pair_A coupling rest lengths 2.4/2.6 cm vs pair_B 4.1 cm; in pair_B the big positive b (5.6, 2.8) may come from a compressed coupling spring.

Hmm, but pair_B is a different device with different offsets; can't share. Still, the point stands qualitatively and is a candidate mechanism. That is a "distinct explanation" contribution — good for disagreement/alternative.

Now: also the "third state" issue. In the collinearity picture, the interior equilibrium at θ = φ = arctan(γ/y) is where the drive torque vanishes. Is it stable? The restoring character depends on (R−ℓ0): if spring in tension (R>ℓ0), torque ∝ −(R−ℓ0)(y sinθ−γcosθ)/R pushes θ toward φ → stable interior equilibrium! If R<ℓ0 (compression), pushes away → unstable. So there can be a genuine *stable third state*: rotor floating at θ = arctan(γ/y) with spring at tension, not touching either stop — and its position tracks γ continuously (no hysteresis at all). The peer's branch clamp_admissibility_limits says "被耦合拉离止挡，成为 ±1 编码看不见的连续角度第三态" — I can now give the precise condition for that third state: rotor leaves stop when the *net* torque (drive+coupling) at the stop pushes it inward, and it can be *captured* by the interior zero (θ ≈ φ_eff, where the effective direction includes the coupling spring's line, i.e., the resultant of the two spring forces passes through the pivot) rather than falling to the other stop, iff the resultant spring force at that configuration is tensile. Excellent — this is a genuine, precise mechanism, and it is exactly the "third state" the peer hypothesized. Removal of the weight makes the scale return to its initial position. Reversibility is an essential feature for this device to function. Now, assume that instead of the kitchen scale you use a sandbag. A weight placed on the sandbag will compress its surface in proportion to it; however, the sandbag lacks the feature of reversibility. Not only will removal of the weight fail to cause a reversion of the bag to its initial shape, but subsequent weights put on the bag will change the current deformation state little, unless you place a heavier weight on it. However, the sandbag does measure something: the largest deformation it has been subjected to in its past. Thus, while the kitchen scale measures a state, the shape of the sandbag provides information about its deformation history. It is a conceptually simple example for memory formation in matter ( 1 ) and demonstrates that the disorder of the grains, as well as the dissipation of energy when the sandbag is deformed, play an essential role in its irreversible behavior. On the other hand, it is precisely this irreversibility which permits one to go from measuring states to measuring histories and thereby encoding memory. In PNAS, Shohat et al. ( 2 ) investigate memory formation in crumpled sheets of paper. Exploring the complex interplay of the geometry and mechanics of wrinkled paper, they demonstrate how memory emerges from the interactions of bistable mechanical instabilities formed by its folds and creases. The findings of Shohat et al. ( 2 ) are remarkable, since they demonstrate in an explicit and experimentally accessible manner how memory can emerge in everyday systems such as a crumpled sheet of paper, thereby contributing toward our understanding of memory formation in driven disordered systems.\\nMemory-recording mechanical devices can be constructed from bistable elements ( 3 ) such as origami bellows ( 4 ), corrugated elastic sheets ( 5 ), and, more generally, mechanical metamaterials ( 6 ). Under a compression, a bistable element remains in one of its stable states, call it “0,” until the force rises above a threshold level  F + , upon which a fast relaxation snap event causes a transition into the other state, “1,” as shown in  Fig. 1  A ,  Top Left . Subsequently reducing the forcing, a transition back into state “0” will occur when the force falls below a threshold level  F − . Hysteresis emerges when the two switching fields  F ±  are such that  F − < F + , so that for values between these two thresholds the actual state of the bistable element depends on the history of the forcing. Such elementary units of hysteresis are called Preisach hysterons ( 7 – 9 ).\\n( A ,  Top Left ) Elementary hysteresis cycle of a Preisach hysteron resulting from a bistable mechanical element with states 0 and 1 under force  F . The hysteron can be in state 1 for  F > F −  and state 0 for  F < F + . In the interval  F − < F < F +  the state depends on the history of the forcing. ( A ,  Center ) The state transition graph of four hysterons each coupling independently to the driving  F . ( A ,  Lower Right ) The ordering of the switching fields  F i ±  is as indicated. Black/gray (red/orange) arrows indicate state changes of the corresponding hysteron  i  when  F  is just above (below)  F i +  ( F i + ). A possible trajectory from 0000 to the state 0101 is shown by the black and red arrows. ( B ,  Top Left ) The experimental set up of ref.  2  for a crumpled sheet of paper driven by a variable strain Δ. ( B ,  Center ) The force–strain response under cyclic straining, once a periodic cycle has set in (yellow cycle). A subsequent driving protocol of the form shown in the lower right inset results in the subcycles shown. Adapted from Shohat et al. ( 2 ). The transition graph ( A ) and the cyclically sheared paper response ( B ) reveal a hierarchy of nested cycles characteristic of RPM.\\nConsider now a collection of  N  hysterons, each with a pair of threshold forces  F i ± , and each coupling independently to the applied force  F . One can construct a history-recording device by ordering the threshold forces as  F 1 + < F 2 + < … < F N +  and  F 1 − > F 2 − > … > F N − , as sketched in  Fig. 1 A ,  Lower Right . Initializing the device in a configuration where each hysteron is in its “0” state, upon increasing the force they will change states one by one in the order  1 , 2 , … , N . Due to the choice of ordering the  F i − , this will be also the same order in which the elements return from their “1” to their “0” state. A state transition graph of this system for the case  N  = 4 is shown in  Fig. 1 A . Here, gray/black (orange/red) arrows indicate transitions when the force has just increased (decreased) enough so that one element becomes unstable and changes state.\\nNote the nesting of cycles in  Fig. 1 A :  Starting from the state 0010, a sequence of gray/black arrows followed by orange/red arrows leads via 1110 back to 0010, forming a graph cycle, which in turn is nested within the cycle between states 0000 and 1110, etc. Observe also that from any state in the graph, by lowering the forcing sufficiently we can “reset” the system by bringing it back to the state 0000. The hierarchical nesting of cycles within cycles is a characteristic feature associated with return-point memory (RPM) ( 10 ), which emerges in the hysteretical magnetization response of magnets to an applied magnetic field. In the transition graph setting, the nesting feature is a topological property of the transitions between hysteron states, which is referred to as loop RPM ( 11 ). Assume now that starting in state 0000 a sequence of forcings leads the system to state 0101. The hierarchical nesting of cycles constrains the possible trajectories that the system must have followed in order to reach 0101 from the zero state: In particular, in the recent past the force must have risen above the value of  F 3 + , subsequently fallen, but not below  F 3 − , then risen again to a value between  F 2 +  and  F 3 + , etc. The shortest trajectory from 0000 to 0101 has been highlighted by the red and black arrows in  Fig. 1 A .\\nRemarkably, mechanical instabilities, which give rise to hysteresis in the form of near-perfect RPM with a hierarchy of nested hysteresis cycles, are rather ubiquitous. They are found in the athermal quasi-static response of various driven disordered systems, such as simulations of amorphous solids under shear strain ( 12 ) and experiments on sheared colloidal suspensions ( 13 ) as well as jammed granular particles under uniaxial compression ( 14 ). In all these systems thermal effects are negligible, and the mechanical instabilities are due to spatially localized plastic events, called soft spots ( 15 – 17 ), which effectively respond as hysterons. However, in contrast to the collection of noninteracting Preisach hysterons, these soft spots interact with each other via long-range elastic deformations. As a result, the state change of one soft spot can alter the switching fields of the other, but it can also give rise to new soft spots or deactivate existing ones by disabling their switching behavior. Overall, these interactions can give rise to highly complex dynamics, including avalanches where the instability of one soft spot triggers instabilities of multiple others, and more generally dynamically critical phenomena, such as yielding. The Preisach model, due to the absence of interactions, lacks all this complexity. Nevertheless, it is a conceptually simple model to illustrate key mechanisms of memory formation, such as RPM, serving a role similar to the ideal gas in statistical mechanics.\\nThe interactions between hysterons turn out to be both a blessing and a curse. They are a curse since in principle interactions can destroy the hierarchical RPM-type nesting of hysteresis cycles and hence adversely affect the capability of memory formation. They are a blessing since the interactions permit a degree of “programmability”: Cyclically driving the system until a periodic response has set in is tantamount to selecting a set of interacting soft spots that “play nice” with each other, i.e., they only moderately influence or impede each other’s switching behavior so that an RPM-like hierarchy of nested cycles remains largely intact.\\nSurprisingly, many of the driven disordered systems mentioned above achieve both the programmability and nesting of hysteresis cycles, and the reasons for this are still not sufficiently understood. Now the paper by Shohat et al. ( 2 ) adds one more such system to the fray: a thin sheet of crumpled paper subject to driving via stretching and unstretching it ( Fig. 1 B ). The relation between the complex geometry of folds and creases of a crumpled sheet of paper and its mechanical response to external driving has so far been largely unexplored. By combining cyclic stretching protocols with three-dimensional (3D) imaging, Shohat et al. ( 2 ) are able to correlate the mechanical response of the sheet to its local geometrical transformation.\\nShohat et al. ( 2 ) find that when the sheet is cyclically strained it settles into a near-perfect periodic force–strain hysteresis cycle dotted with a large number of abrupt force jumps. Using 3D imaging, Shohat et al. ( 2 ) are able to trace the force jumps to localized plastic events in the sheet, originating from the snapping of vertices formed by the crossings of ridges ( 18 ). Shohat et al. ( 2 ) demonstrate that these mechanical instabilities behave as hysterons that interact with each other. As in the sheared amorphous solids, depending on the locations and states of the other hysterons, the interactions can facilitate or impede each other’s switching behavior. The sheet of paper has become a mechanical realization of a spin glass, an archetypical model for understanding the emergence of complexity in disordered systems ( 19 ).\\nThese findings set the stage for a thorough investigation of memory formation. First, Shohat et al. ( 2 ) “program” their sheet of paper by applying cyclic strain over a strain range  [ Δ 0 min , Δ 0 max ]  until a periodic response is attained in the force–strain response of the sheet ( Fig. 1 B ). The response to cyclic deformation has all the hallmarks of RPM. Once a periodic response has set in, a subsequent reduction of  Δ 0 max  to  Δ 1 max  results in force-versus-strain subcycles of the original hysteresis cycle, as depicted in  Fig. 1 B . In fact, the amplitude  Δ 1 max  can be lowered and raised as long as  Δ 1 max ≤ Δ 0 max , i.e., it does not exceed the value at which the original hysteresis cycle was obtained. Raising  Δ 1 max  back to  Δ 0 max , the original cycle is recovered. Thus, applying oscillatory shear to the crumpled paper has led to the selection of an interacting hysteron system that supports a hierarchy of cycles and subcycles, as shown in  Fig. 1 B . As in simulations of sheared amorphous solids ( 12 ), the emergence of the interacting hysteron system is at the heart of the memory that is imprinted into the disordered system as a result of cyclic loading. In fact, raising  Δ 1 max  to a value above  Δ 0 max  and then back to  Δ 0 max , Shohat et al. ( 2 ) show that this memory is erased.\\nThe relative ease with which the interacting hysterons of a driven disordered system establish a hierarchy of nested hysteresis cycles suggests that this may not have to be a consequence of the cyclic driving. The approximate rate independence of the response implies that the duration of the driving cycle is not important, while the hierarchy of nested cycles suggests that the driving need not be periodic, as long as it is confined to some range, e.g., the interval  [ Δ 0 min , Δ 0 max ]  in the case of the crumpled sheet.
